opus-5.5.text:
I think the limitations are quite severe, honestly. When people try to reason about AI capabilities from first principles, they usually start from some story about what intelligence is, or what a particular task "really requires," and then try to deduce whether a given system can or can't do it. The track record of that kind of reasoning has been pretty poor.

If you'd asked people ten or fifteen years ago which tasks would fall first, many would have said routine physical work, then simple cognitive work, with creative or open-ended reasoning last. What we've seen is closer to the opposite. Language models write poetry, code, and explain complicated ideas, while robotics and reliable long-horizon agency remain hard. That's essentially Moravec's paradox reasserting itself, and I don't think first-principles arguments did a good job anticipating it.

Part of the problem is that our intuitions about difficulty come from what's hard for humans, and that's a poor guide to what's hard for a learning system trained on a particular data distribution with a particular amount of compute. Things that feel effortless to us, like perception and motor control, rest on hundreds of millions of years of evolutionary optimization. Things that feel hard, like formal reasoning, may be computationally cheaper than they seem.

So I tend to put much more weight on empirical approaches: scaling laws, compute trends, looking at how benchmark performance has improved as a function of inputs, and extrapolating, with appropriate humility. Those methods have their own problems. Benchmarks saturate, they may not measure what we care about, and trends can break. But they've been more reliable than armchair arguments about what neural networks fundamentally can't do. Many confident claims of that form, that deep learning can't do compositional reasoning or that language models will never handle some task, have aged badly.

I don't think first-principles reasoning is useless. It's valuable for generating hypotheses, and some constraints, like physical limits on compute or the cost of collecting real-world data, are worth reasoning about carefully. But when a first-principles argument conflicts with a clear empirical trend, I'd usually bet on the trend. The burden of proof should be on the person claiming a trend is about to stop, and they should point to something concrete, like running out of data or compute becoming prohibitively expensive, rather than an intuition that the system doesn't "really understand."

fable-5.1.text:
I think first-principles prediction of AI capabilities is a lot weaker than people often assume, and the reason is that we don't actually have a theory of what makes a given capability hard or easy for these systems. If you had asked people in 2015 to rank tasks by difficulty, most would have said something like: chess is easy, Go is hard, protein structure prediction is very hard, and writing a decent essay or passing the bar exam is basically science fiction. And the actual order in which these things fell was almost unrelated to that ranking. So the track record of people reasoning from intuitions about what's cognitively difficult is just bad.

What has worked much better is extrapolating trends. If you look at compute scaling, loss curves, benchmark performance as a function of training compute, those have been fairly regular, and people who just drew the line forward did better than people who tried to argue from the nature of intelligence. But the trend-extrapolation approach has its own limits, because the benchmarks saturate, the thing you're measuring stops being informative, and you have to keep inventing new proxies for what you actually care about. And the mapping from "the model gets better on this benchmark" to "the model can do economically meaningful work" is itself something we don't understand from first principles.

So the honest position, I think, is that we can say with reasonable confidence that capabilities will keep improving as long as the inputs keep scaling, and we can say something about the rate. What we can't do very well is say which specific capabilities arrive when, or what the system will look like qualitatively. Anyone claiming to derive that from the architecture or from some argument about what deep learning fundamentally can't do, I'd discount pretty heavily. Those arguments have mostly been wrong, and not in a way that suggests the next one will be right.

astra-6.text:
I think first-principles reasoning can give you some useful constraints, but it’s much harder to get a precise prediction out of it. There’s a big gap between saying that a capability is possible in principle and saying that a particular training run will produce it at a particular cost.

For that second question, you need to know things about the data, the learning algorithm, and how efficiently the model can learn the relevant task. Those are often exactly the things we don’t understand well enough to derive an answer from first principles. So you can have an argument that sounds quite compelling but depends on an assumption that turns out to be wrong.

I would put more weight on empirical trends, while recognizing that those have limitations too. If you see predictable improvements as you increase compute, that gives you a basis for extrapolation. But translating that into a prediction about, say, when a system can autonomously do scientific research requires additional assumptions.

So I’d use first-principles arguments to check whether a forecast makes sense and to identify possible constraints. I’d be much more skeptical of using them to establish a precise timeline or a hard limit on what AI can do.

sol-6.1.text:
I think first-principles reasoning is useful for identifying constraints, but it’s much less useful for telling you exactly when a particular capability will appear. You can reason about how much compute is available, how much data you have, or how expensive training is going to be. But there’s a substantial gap between those quantities and whether a model can reliably do some economically important task.

Part of the problem is that we don’t have a sufficiently good theory of intelligence to derive those capabilities. You can observe that loss improves predictably as you scale a model, but translating that into a prediction about its ability to do research, for example, requires additional empirical evidence. The predictability of the loss doesn’t automatically give you predictability of everything you care about.

So I would put more weight on empirical trends, while being careful about how far we extrapolate them. First-principles arguments can help you check whether a forecast is plausible, or identify where a trend must eventually break. But I’d be skeptical of arguments that claim to establish a very specific timeline just from some general fact about computation or the human brain. There are too many things in between that we don’t understand well enough.
